Unlawful
ŭn-lô´fụl
adj. (contrary to law; not permitted; rendering Greek athemitos and anomos)
Un + lawful. The Greek of Acts 10:28 is athemitos, contrary to what is established — and the thing Peter calls unlawful there is a rule of men, not of God.

Biblical Definition

Peter in the house of Cornelius: “Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation; but God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean” (Act 10:28). Of Lot in Sodom: that righteous man “vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds” (2Pe 2:8). The Lord answered the sabbath charge — “Behold, thy disciples do that which is not lawful to do upon the sabbath day” (Mat 12:2) — from David and the shewbread and from the priests in the temple, and concluded, “it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days” (Mat 12:12).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines unlawful as not lawful; contrary to law; illegal; not permitted by law; and, of an act, contrary to the moral law or divine command.

expand to see more

UNLAWFUL, a. Not lawful; contrary to law; illegal; not permitted by law; as an unlawful act.

2. Not moral; contrary to the divine law.

3. Illegitimate; born out of wedlock.

Key Scripture

Act 10:28 — "And he said unto them, Ye know how that it is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew to keep company, or come unto one of another nation; but God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean."

2Pe 2:8 — "(For that righteous man dwelling among them, in seeing and hearing, vexed his righteous soul from day to day with their unlawful deeds;)"

Mat 12:2 — "But when the Pharisees saw it, they said unto him, Behold, thy disciples do that which is not lawful to do upon the sabbath day."

Mat 12:12 — "How much then is a man better than a sheep? Wherefore it is lawful to do well on the sabbath days."

1Co 6:12 — "All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any."

Modern Corruption

Human rules are enforced as divine law, and Peter calls the rule that kept him out of Cornelius's house unlawful in exactly that sense.

expand to see more

Acts 10:28 is a careful sentence and the care is easy to miss. Peter says it is an unlawful thing for a Jew to keep company with a Gentile — and no such law exists in Moses. It was a fence, a scruple built up around the clean and unclean legislation, held so long and so universally that it had the force of divine command in the conscience of every Jew in the room, Peter included, until the sheet came down three times. The passage is therefore the standing warning about the tradition that has hardened into law: sincerity is no protection, near-unanimity is no protection, and it took a vision repeated three times to move an apostle off it.

The Lord's sabbath controversies work the same seam. The Pharisees said not lawful of plucking corn and of healing, and He met them with Scripture rather than with sentiment — David ate the shewbread, the priests profane the sabbath and are blameless, and the sabbath was made for man. The lawful and the unlawful are decided by the Lawgiver and are found in the text; where the text is silent the conscience is free, and a church that binds it there has usurped a jurisdiction.

First Corinthians 6:12 guards the other flank, and Paul is quoting a slogan the Corinthians had got from him and stretched: all things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient. Liberty is real and it is not the last word; the free man asks not only whether a thing is permitted but whether it profits and whether it will bring him under its power. Between the fence that binds where God has not and the licence that will not ask a second question, the New Testament walks a narrow road.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek athemitos (G111), contrary to what is laid down, unlawful; anomos (G459), lawless, without law; exestin (G1832), it is lawful, permitted.

expand to see more

Greek athemitos (G111) — unlawful; Acts 10:28, 1 Peter 4:3 only.

Greek anomos (G459) — lawless, unlawful; 2 Peter 2:8, 1 Timothy 1:9, 2 Thessalonians 2:8.

Greek exestin (G1832) — it is lawful; Matthew 12:2, 12:10, 12:12, 1 Corinthians 6:12, 10:23.

Usage

"“It is an unlawful thing for a man that is a Jew” — a rule with no verse behind it."

"“It is lawful to do well on the sabbath days” — the Lawgiver settling His own law."

"“All things are lawful… but all things are not expedient” — the second question."
